title: This 1987 Monte Carlo SS Hot Rod Runs “Cleaner and Meaner”

body_markdown:
When I mat the Monte’s gas pedal, the old coupe rears back on its haunches. A moment of silence, then the torque-converter four-speed automatic kicks down, ready to take a fat dose of V-8 torque. Magnaflows soon pump out the LS motor’s steady snarl as the rear tires hook up and launch the 1987 G-body toward the horizon. The speedometer needle climbs. And climbs. Upshifts happen with punch, authority, as if shouting, “I DID NOT STUTTER, SIR.” Once satisfied, I all but stand on the brakes, bringing the car to a screeching halt. No drama, no wonky or wobbly brake dive.


A Monte Carlo SS, yes, but this Pro Touring hot rod built by Summit Racing, the Ohio-based parts house, is a different beast altogether than stock. This Monte puts down power better, handles better, stops better. Most people hear “hot rod” and imagine a blubbering, smoking heap that prioritizes performance over efficiency or emissions. With this project, Summit set out to prove that modern hot-rodding can improve both power output and cleanliness. Their target: double the ponies, half the emissions. Or, in Summit Racing Restoration Category Lead Barry Flesher’s words, “a whole lot cleaner and a whole lot meaner.”


[Eric Weiner](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/eric-weiner/)


[Eric Weiner](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/eric-weiner/)


[Eric Weiner](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/eric-weiner/)


Eric Weiner


As Flesher explained to us at the SEMA Garage Detroit, where we met Summit’s team and the Monte Carlo, the idea for this project started brewing in 2017. At the time, EPA emissions regulations went into effect, limiting the practice of fitting “glider kit” Class A transport trucks—essentially a semi sold sans powertrain—with aftermarket or rebuilt engines. The language of the law, however, was vague enough to also apply to ordinary passenger vehicles, which would have had a profound effect on the business of aftermarket engine swaps.


The law was ultimately clarified, ensuring that automotive engine swaps could continue unabated, but about three years ago, Summit went ahead with its proof of concept to drive home the point that hot-rodding a car could also yield cleaner emissions. Over that time, the Monte Carlo SS went through numerous phases, including three different engines. As changes took place, Summit measured performance and particulates from each iteration of the build at SEMA Garage Detroit—a fully certified testing facility with a dyno, OEM-level emissions testing equipment, and a whole lot more. Almost every single part for the project came from Summit’s catalog.


[Eric Weiner](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/eric-weiner/)


[Eric Weiner](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/eric-weiner/)


Why a Monte Carlo, though? “We were looking for an emissions-era vehicle that an enthusiast might want—nothing exotic, unattainable, or unrelatable,” Flesher said. “Everybody has a Monte Carlo memory. Like going to a Poison concert in ‘88, or something.”


Summit’s lead wrench on the Monte was Justin Weideman, Technical Lead and Video Host—a man whose parents drove him home from the hospital in a white ‘87 Monte Carlo. When Weideman and team located a candidate in Dayton, Ohio, they sprang into action. “It was granny-fresh, all original and factory-correct. It was a survivor car around 97,000 miles, and we bought it for $12,500.”


[Eric Weiner](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/eric-weiner/)


## Phase 1: Baseline Testing


From the factory, the ‘87 Monte Carlo SS came with a 305-cubic-inch (5.0-liter) V-8, fitted with a computer-controlled four-barrel Rochester carburetor. It was factory-rated for 180 hp and came with a catalytic converter.


After testing the survivor Monte, it came back with 131 hp at the wheels and about 150 hp at the crank. Degraded performance is common over time, and Summit found a sticking carb choke, leaking valve seals, a cracked block, and decreased performance from the OEM catalyst compared with stock. Though none of this is optimal from a performance perspective, it set a reasonable baseline for the type of project car most hot-rodders might begin with.


## Phase 2: EFI Conversion


The next step was an attempt to retain the factory 305 engine while improving horsepower. Out went the carb in favor of Summit Max-EFI 500 throttle-body injection. Along with it: a new fuel tank, pump, and regulator.


Improvements were minimal here, amounting to a 3% uptick in horsepower.


[Eric Weiner](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/eric-weiner/)


## Phase 3: Typical Hot-Rodder Tweaks


Nothing too fancy here for 305 upgrades: a dual-plane intake manifold, new exhaust system, timing advanced from six degrees to ten, and long-tube headers with three-inch “high-flow” catalysts. The factory secondary air injection and exhaust gas recirculation systems weren’t working, so Weideman removed them.


Combining EFI injection with the aforementioned tweaks ratcheted up horsepower by 40 from stock, totaling about 172 whp. (Interestingly, output was 8% better with catalytic converters than without.)


On the emissions side, the additional horsepower came at the cost of even worse emissions. And, to top it off, the factory catalytic converter actually reduced emissions better than the aftermarket pieces from Stainless Works.


## Phase 4: Blueprint Power


[Brandan Gillogly](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/brandan-gillogly/)


Summit’s next step was a brand-new 383-cu-in small-block V-8 from Blueprint Engines, fitted with the intake, injection setup, and OEM ignition control used in Phase 3. This time, Weideman tried a variety of header and catalytic converter combinations.


Best performance came from short-tube headers with Magnaflow cats, ultimately increasing wheel horsepower from 172 to 268 between Phases 3 and 4. That meant double the horsepower from Phase 1, with emissions vastly improved but not quite on target: Total Hydrocarbon Content (THC) was down 80%, and nitrogen oxides (NOx) were down 71%. Phase 4 represents a solid accomplishment on its own; one that represents a healthy dose of power for a G-Body and an admirable reduction in emissions, all by sticking with an old-school small-block.


But the team wasn’t quite done yet.


## Phase 5: LS It


[Eric Weiner](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/eric-weiner/)


When in doubt, LS swap.


Weideman, aiming for what he calls a “mild budget build,” chose Summit’s 5.3-liter LS V-8—the same type of engine you’d find in a 25-year-old Chevy truck. “In hot-rodding terms, this is a modest, easily sourced powerplant,” he told us. “We added a 24x crank trigger, ECU from a 2002 Camaro, and a Trick Flow Specialties (TFS) Dyno map, plus a mild 222°/231°-112° LSA camshaft.”


The result: 302 horsepower at the wheels, or 2.3 times the baseline measurement of the vintage 305. If that seems low, it’s because the four-speed transmission’s shift point limits the revs before the max output of roughly 400 hp.


[Eric Weiner](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/eric-weiner/)


With this engine and GESI High Load catalytic converters, compared with baseline, THC went down 81%, carbon monoxide (CO) was down 93%, and NOx was down 71%.


The numbers don’t tell the full story, either. Weideman articulated: “When people think emissions equipment, they just think catalytic converters. You don’t think about all the other parts. So for example, on the Monte Carlo, we put a complete aftermarket vapor canister setup on it. So it still has a full PCV setup with an aftermarket vapor guard vapor canister in the back, and that’s all plumbed into the car. You can tell when a car doesn’t have cats. We’ve all parked a carbureted car inside a garage, and then you walk out in the morning, and that’s all you smell.”


## Pro Touring Time


[Eric Weiner](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/eric-weiner/)


With the team’s power and emissions goals realized, it was time to upgrade the rest of the Monte Carlo to match.


“We aimed for a Pro Touring-flavor build with the LS swap and an aftermarket suspension, which gives it that stance,” noted Flesher.


Chassis upgrades include a Level 2 suspension kit from QA1: that’s front control arms with adjustable coilovers, rear trailing arms with adjustable coils and shocks, frame bracing, and anti-roll bars for the front and rear. Wilwood supplied the braking setup, with four-piston front calipers and vented rotors nestled inside Forgeline wheels. The steering system received a fresh box and shaft kit.


[Eric Weiner](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/eric-weiner/)


For the drivetrain, Weideman wanted to retain the four-speed transmission and same 3.73 rear end. The 200-4R unit was rebuilt and resealed, along with a new torque converter with lockup, TransGo shift kit, cooler, driveshaft, and Mosier Muscle Pak 12-bolt rear end.


“Everything we did could be completed by a home enthusiast with basic hand tools, a little welding, and some ingenuity,” he declared. “I had this thing completely apart and reassembled many times. I took it on Hot Rod Power Tour and ran from Chicago down to Tulsa and back. I also did Summit Racing Autocross weekend this year, driving from Ohio to the Nashville area, and ran four different days on four different courses. I left the truck and trailer at home and put it on the road and drove it. That’s what people want to see.”


Summit Racing


All told, the bill for Phase 5 rang in at just north of $45,000 in parts. Not nothing, to be sure, but far from a six-figure custom hot rod, even with the $12,500 purchase price of the baseline Monte Carlo SS factored in.


## Modernized Muscle


[Eric Weiner](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/eric-weiner/)


The Monte is a lovely piece of kit, combining relatively modern technology with a distinct 1980s flavor. The interior is largely untouched, aside from new bucket seats, a rear chassis brace, steering wheel, and an aftermarket gauge cluster.


The 5.3 fires up willingly when we turn the ignition key. The sound is throaty but still civilized, and it idles happily after ten or fifteen seconds. Throttle takes a bit of foot pressure to urge on the V-8, but once it’s in the mid-range the LS sings. Upshifts are a bit harsh, though not out of character for an ‘80s GM four-speed with a shift kit. The harder you are on it, the smoother it shifts. Even at the top of the rev range, the pushrod motor pulls strong. On the road, the Monte Carlo is fast enough to be fun but never unruly or unwieldy.


[Eric Weiner](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/eric-weiner/)


Steering feels more precise and accurate the more angle you have into it. The on-center feel is a little loose, much like C10 trucks of the era. The nose takes a moment to catch up to inputs, but the Monte corners flat and handles bumps small or large without consequence. None of these shortfalls are necessarily bad—a G-body should still feel like a G-body, and this ‘87 SS does.


[Eric Weiner](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/eric-weiner/)


We smile after a few hard pulls, praising Weideman for his handiwork. He’s grateful:


“People who don’t understand hot rodding think we just all drive dirty junk down the road. But even when it’s old stuff, hot rodders pay better attention to maintenance than a lot of people do with their daily drivers. We wanted to show that it was possible to build something that was a bit old, a bit new, and clean.”


Mission accomplished, fellas.
